# Context Engineering and Harness Engineering {#context-harness-engineering}

## Why these two terms matter

Earlier chapters covered prompting, verification loops, hooks, skills, and MCP
as separate techniques. Two newer terms give those techniques a common frame:

- **Context engineering** asks: *which tokens should the model see at this
  step?* It covers instructions, retrieved data, tool definitions, tool
  outputs, conversation history, and memory.
- **Harness engineering** asks: *what system around the model makes it reliable
  over many steps?* It covers the agent loop, tools, sandbox, state files,
  hooks, permissions, tests, and evaluation.

Both terms are young, and their boundaries are still debated. This chapter
separates three kinds of claim: concepts that are likely to last, vendor
practices and features that change quickly, and evidence. The evidence is
labeled by strength throughout.

**Source labels used in this chapter**

- **[Vendor]**: an organization reporting on its own product or results.
- **[Secondary]**: the original could not be read; the claim comes from a
  mirror, summary, or aggregator.
- **[Unverified]**: no primary source was found.

Product names, API identifiers, and preview status are as of October 2026.

## Where the terms came from

### Context engineering (mid-2025)

The term spread through a cluster of posts in June and July 2025. No single
person has a verified claim to coining it, so "popularized by" is the accurate
phrasing.

- Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke described it as "the art of providing all the context
  for the task to be plausibly solvable by the LLM" (June 2025, quoted by
  [Simon Willison](https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jun/27/context-engineering/)).
- Harrison Chase of LangChain defined it as building dynamic systems that give
  the model "the right information and tools in the right format," and credited
  earlier practitioners
  ([LangChain](https://www.langchain.com/blog/the-rise-of-context-engineering)).
- Andrej Karpathy called it "the delicate art and science of filling the context
  window with just the right information for the next step." He compared the
  model to a CPU and the context window to its RAM (June 2025, quoted by
  [Simon Willison](https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jun/27/context-engineering/)).
- Drew Breunig named common ways long contexts fail
  ([How contexts fail](https://www.dbreunig.com/2025/06/22/how-contexts-fail-and-how-to-fix-them.html);
  [How to fix your context](https://www.dbreunig.com/2025/06/26/how-to-fix-your-context.html)).
- Manus published lessons from running a production agent
  ([Manus, July 2025](https://manus.im/blog/Context-Engineering-for-AI-Agents-Lessons-from-Building-Manus)).
- Anthropic's engineering guide (29 September 2025) gave the most-cited
  definition: strategies for curating and maintaining the optimal set of tokens
  during LLM inference
  ([Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents)).

### Harness engineering (early 2026)

"Harness" and "scaffold" already meant the code around a model. The phrase
*harness engineering* became common in early 2026.

- Phil Schmid (January 2026) described the agent harness as the infrastructure
  that wraps a model to manage long-running tasks, and said it is not the agent
  itself. He extended Karpathy's analogy: model = CPU, context = RAM,
  harness = operating system, agent = application
  ([philschmid.de](https://www.philschmid.de/agent-harness-2026)).
- Mitchell Hashimoto (February 2026) gave the most practical definition:
  whenever an agent makes a mistake, engineer a fix so it never makes that
  mistake again. His fixes were updates to `AGENTS.md` plus small,
  purpose-built scripts
  ([mitchellh.com](https://mitchellh.com/writing/my-ai-adoption-journey)).
- OpenAI published "Harness engineering: leveraging Codex in an agent-first
  world" (February 2026). It describes a team that designs the environment
  while agents write the code
  ([OpenAI](https://openai.com/index/harness-engineering/)). **[Secondary]**:
  the page could not be read for this chapter. Its widely repeated figures
  (code volume, team size, number of pull requests) are therefore not
  reproduced here.
- LangChain summarized the idea as "Agent = Model + Harness"
  ([LangChain, March 2026](https://www.langchain.com/blog/the-anatomy-of-an-agent-harness)).
- Birgitta Böckeler's article on martinfowler.com (April 2026) reframed harness
  engineering for teams that *use* coding agents
  ([martinfowler.com](https://martinfowler.com/articles/exploring-gen-ai/harness-engineering.html)).
- Anthropic documented harness patterns for long-running agents
  ([November 2025](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-harnesses-for-long-running-agents);
  [March 2026](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/harness-design-long-running-apps))
  **[Vendor]**.

These definitions emphasize different things. Hashimoto's is incremental,
OpenAI's is organizational, Schmid's and LangChain's are architectural, and
Böckeler's treats the harness as a control system.

## How prompt, context, and harness relate

| Layer | Question it answers | Typical artifacts |
|---|---|---|
| Prompt engineering | How should the instruction be worded? | System prompt, few-shot examples |
| Context engineering | Which tokens should the model see at this step? | Retrieval, tool selection, compaction, memory files, sub-agent summaries |
| Harness engineering | What system makes the model reliable over many steps? | Agent loop, sandbox, hooks, tests and linters, evaluator agents, state logs, permissions |

LangChain calls prompt engineering "a subset of context engineering," and
Anthropic calls context engineering its "natural progression." Treat the chain
*prompt ⊂ context ⊂ harness* as a **teaching heuristic**, not a settled
taxonomy: it appears mostly in explainers, not in primary lab writing.

The more precise statement is that the harness *contains* context management,
but it also includes deterministic machinery, such as linters, sandboxes, and
permission checks. That machinery affects the model only when its output is
fed back into the context.

**Is it just a rebrand?** In part. Retrieval, summarization, and RAG all
predate the label, and some experienced developers dismiss the term as
rebranded prompt engineering
([Addy Osmani](https://addyo.substack.com/p/context-engineering-bringing-engineering)).
What is new is treating these techniques as **one budgeted design problem for
multi-step agents**, which a prompt-only view hides.

## Context engineering

### Context is a finite attention budget

The founding premise is that *more context can make results worse*. Anthropic
describes a finite "attention budget" and names **context rot**: recall falls
as the token count grows. The goal it sets is "the smallest set of high-signal
tokens" that makes the desired outcome likely.

Evidence:

- **Lost in the middle.** Accuracy was highest when the relevant information sat
  at the beginning or end of a long input, and worse in the middle
  ([Liu et al., arXiv 2307.03172](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172)).
- **Context rot.** Across 18 models, performance degraded as input length grew,
  often unevenly
  ([Chroma, July 2025](https://www.trychroma.com/research/context-rot)).
  **[Vendor]**: Chroma sells retrieval infrastructure, and the study is not peer
  reviewed.

A practical consequence: a larger advertised context window is a capacity
limit, not a promise that the model will use every token equally well.

### Four ways context fails

Breunig's taxonomy pairs each failure with a fix. The examples he cites are
secondhand and were not checked against the original papers for this chapter.

| Failure | What happens | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| **Poisoning** | A hallucination or error enters context and is reused as if true | Validate before writing to memory; prune; quarantine |
| **Distraction** | A long history crowds out the task; the agent repeats past actions | Summarize or compact; start fresh with a handoff note |
| **Confusion** | Irrelevant tools or documents degrade choices | Load fewer tools; retrieve selectively |
| **Clash** | New information contradicts earlier context | Remove stale content; keep one source of truth |

### Four families of technique: write, select, compress, isolate

LangChain groups the techniques into four families
([LangChain](https://www.langchain.com/blog/context-engineering-for-agents)).

1. **Write: persist state outside the window.** Scratchpads, progress notes, and
   to-do files let an agent recover after its history is trimmed. Manus has the
   agent rewrite a `todo.md` so its goals stay at the *end* of the context, a
   direct counter to lost-in-the-middle.
2. **Select: retrieve just in time.** Keep lightweight identifiers (file paths,
   table names, saved queries) and load content only when needed. Claude Code
   combines an up-front `CLAUDE.md` with on-demand file search. Selection
   applies to tools too: a smaller, relevant toolset reduces confusion.
3. **Compress: summarize or prune.** Compaction replaces old history with a
   summary that keeps decisions, open issues, and key details, and drops
   redundant tool output.
4. **Isolate: give sub-tasks clean windows.** A sub-agent explores in its own
   context and returns a short summary (Anthropic suggests roughly 1,000 to
   2,000 tokens). Isolation costs extra tokens, and some practitioners argue
   that splitting work across agents fragments shared understanding. Choose it
   for parallel, separable work, not by default.

Supporting guidance from the
[Anthropic guide](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents):

- Write system prompts at the "right altitude": specific enough to guide
  behavior, but heuristic rather than a brittle list of rules.
- Use a few diverse, canonical examples rather than every edge case.
- Make tools self-contained, robust to errors, and clearly distinct from one
  another. Return compact tool outputs, not raw dumps.

### Cost: the overlooked dimension

Agents read far more tokens than they write. Manus reports a ratio of roughly
100 input tokens per output token and calls the KV-cache hit rate the most
important production metric **[Vendor]**. Cached input tokens are much cheaper
than uncached ones, which leads to rules such as:

- keep the prompt prefix stable (a timestamp at the top breaks the cache);
- append to the context rather than editing earlier turns;
- serialize JSON deterministically; and
- disable tools by masking them rather than removing their definitions.

These rules **conflict** with compaction and dynamic tool removal, which
invalidate the cache. Good designs compress rarely and in large steps rather
than continuously.

Manus also advises leaving failed attempts in context so the model avoids
repeating them, which seems to contradict "poisoning." One reasonable
reconciliation (the author's judgment): *observed* error messages are useful
feedback, while *unverified claims stored as facts* are harmful.

### Context features are becoming platform features

Vendors now ship these techniques as features, for example Anthropic's
[context editing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-editing),
[memory tool](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool),
[server-side compaction](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/compaction),
and the progressive disclosure built into Agent Skills
(Chapter \@ref(claude-code-skills)). Learn the four families. The API names
will change, but the families will still apply.

## Harness engineering

### What is in a harness

A short working definition: **the harness is everything except the model
weights.** LangChain's list includes system prompts; tools, skills, and MCP
servers (Chapter \@ref(model-context-protocol)); infrastructure such as a
filesystem, sandbox, or browser; orchestration such as sub-agents and model
routing; and hooks or middleware for deterministic steps
([LangChain](https://www.langchain.com/blog/the-anatomy-of-an-agent-harness)).

It helps to separate:

- the **builder harness**: the product runtime (Claude Code, the Claude Agent
  SDK, Codex, LangChain Deep Agents, a custom agent); and
- the **user harness**: what *your team* adds on top, such as `AGENTS.md`,
  specs, tests, linters, hooks, permissions, and CI.

Most data scientists work mainly on the user harness, or build a small builder
harness inside an application.

### Guides and sensors

Böckeler classifies harness controls on two axes
([martinfowler.com](https://martinfowler.com/articles/exploring-gen-ai/harness-engineering.html)):

| | **Computational** (deterministic, cheap, reliable) | **Inferential** (model-based, slower, non-deterministic) |
|---|---|---|
| **Guides** (before the agent acts) | Templates, schemas, scaffolding scripts, type definitions | `AGENTS.md`, specs, feature lists, skills |
| **Sensors** (after the agent acts) | Tests, linters, type checks, schema validation, data-quality checks | AI code review, LLM judges, evaluator agents |

Prefer computational sensors wherever they can answer the question, and use
inferential ones for judgments that code cannot make. Böckeler also notes the
limits: tests do not catch a misdiagnosed problem, over-engineering, or a
misunderstood instruction.

### Each pattern fixes a named failure

| Recurring failure | Harness response | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Declares success too early | Feature list where every item starts "failing"; checklist before exit; stop hooks that require evidence | Anthropic (Nov 2025), LangChain [Vendor] |
| Tries to do everything at once | Work on one feature per session; commit after each | Anthropic (Nov 2025) [Vendor] |
| Edits tests to pass | Explicit rule against changing tests; protected test files; CI | Anthropic (Nov 2025) [Vendor] |
| Loses track over long runs | Progress log, setup script, descriptive commits, handoff notes | Anthropic (Nov 2025) [Vendor] |
| Praises its own mediocre work | A separate evaluator agent that exercises the result | Anthropic (Mar 2026) [Vendor] |
| Repeats the same failing edit | Loop detection that interrupts the agent | LangChain (Feb 2026) [Vendor] |
| Repeats a known mistake | Add a rule to `AGENTS.md` or a deterministic check | Hashimoto (Feb 2026) |

**Documentation is part of the harness, and long documents rot.** Several
practitioners, OpenAI reportedly among them **[Secondary]**, replaced one large
instruction file with a short index that points to focused documents. This is
the same idea as progressive disclosure in skills and just-in-time retrieval.

**Security gaps.** The primary harness posts reviewed say little about
permissions, sandboxing, secret handling, or prompt injection through tool
outputs. Treat these as first-class harness components anyway: apply least
privilege, require human approval for actions that write, spend, or send, and
keep secrets out of context (see Chapters \@ref(claude-code-hooks) and
\@ref(model-context-protocol)).

### The thin-harness debate

Rich Sutton's "Bitter Lesson" argues that general methods that scale with
compute eventually beat hand-built cleverness. Applied to agents, it raises the
question of whether harness logic is a temporary crutch.

- **Thin-harness view.** Anthropic writes that every harness component
  "encodes an assumption about what the model can't do on its own." When a
  stronger model arrived, it removed parts of its own harness
  ([Anthropic, March 2026](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/harness-design-long-running-apps))
  **[Vendor]**. Schmid recommends harnesses that make yesterday's clever logic
  easy to delete.
- **Harness-matters view.** With the model held fixed, LangChain changed only
  its harness and raised its Terminal-Bench 2.0 score from 52.8% to 66.5%
  ([LangChain](https://www.langchain.com/blog/improving-deep-agents-with-harness-engineering))
  **[Vendor]**. A May 2026 position paper argues that harness-induced variance
  can exceed model-induced variance and can reverse model rankings
  ([arXiv 2605.23950](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23950)); it is an argument,
  not a controlled meta-analysis.

The two views are compatible. *Specific* components (elaborate prompts, rigid
step structures, large tool collections) are absorbed as models improve. The
*need* for an environment, verification, persistent state, and permissions
remains.

**Practical implication:** a leaderboard score measures a model–harness pair.
When you compare models for your own application, hold the harness constant,
and when you change the harness, hold the model constant.

### Evaluation is a harness too

Anthropic's guide to agent evaluation distinguishes the *evaluation harness*
from the *agent harness* and defines tasks, trials, graders, transcripts, and
outcomes
([Anthropic, January 2026](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents)):

- **Graders** can be code-based (tests, exact match, schema checks), model-based
  (rubrics, pairwise comparison), or human (expert review).
- **Grade outcomes, not paths.** Judge what the agent produced, but keep
  transcripts for debugging and for spotting reward hacking, such as an agent
  editing the tests it is graded on.
- **pass@k versus pass^k.** pass@k is the chance that *at least one* of *k*
  attempts succeeds; pass^k is the chance that *all k* succeed. For a
  production tool that users run repeatedly, pass^k is the more honest
  reliability measure.

For a statistician, this is familiar ground: define the estimand (task
success), use repeated trials to estimate variance, and avoid grading on the
training set (tasks the harness was tuned on).

## Applying both to Databricks analytics apps

The design principle that follows from the evidence is:

> **The model chooses and explains; governed engines compute; sensors verify.**

This is the author's synthesis rather than an official Databricks rule, but
each part has support in the sources above.

### Metadata is the highest-return context

Text-to-SQL research suggests that semantic context often matters more than
which frontier model you pick:

- Adding a 4 KB semantic-layer document raised accuracy on 100 retail questions
  from about 46–51% to about 68–69% across three frontier models, and the
  differences between models were not statistically significant in either
  condition
  ([arXiv 2604.25149](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.25149)). This is a single study
  on one domain.
- On the BIRD benchmark, better column descriptions improved accuracy, although
  ambiguous columns still needed expert input
  ([arXiv 2408.04691](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.04691)).
- Automatically profiled metadata helped one team reach the top of the BIRD
  leaderboard
  ([arXiv 2505.19988](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.19988)).

Databricks' own Genie guidance is a context-engineering playbook
([Genie best practices](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/genie/best-practices)):

1. Rely on clear Unity Catalog table and column names and descriptions.
2. Start with a small number of tables (the docs suggest five or fewer).
3. Prefer **SQL expressions** for metrics, filters, and dimensions, then
   **example SQL** for complex questions, and use plain-text instructions only
   as a last resort.

[Unity Catalog metric views](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/uc-semantics/metric-views/)
define each measure once (reach, overlap rate, lift, support, confidence) so
that every app and agent computes it the same way.

For an analytics team, this is good news: the highest-return work is data
governance work you may already own. Column comments, metric definitions, and
verified example queries now have a new consumer.

### Mapping to the three workloads

| Workload | Context engineering | Harness engineering | Evaluation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Streamlit analytical apps** on Databricks Apps | Send aggregates (top-N, group-bys, summary statistics), not audience-level rows. Keep few tables in scope. Keep a stable system-prompt prefix | On-behalf-of-user auth so Unity Catalog row filters and column masks apply per user. The model proposes SQL or tool parameters; tables and charts render from the result DataFrame, not from model text | A code check that every number in the narrative appears in the result table; an LLM judge for groundedness |
| **Reusable jobs** (lookalike, audience overlap, basket analysis) | Unity Catalog comments on seed, segment, and transaction tables; metric views for overlap, lift, support, and confidence; a few verified example queries for tricky logic such as fiscal calendars | Expose validated logic as Unity Catalog functions or job-triggering tools via MCP. For coding agents that maintain the job code, a short `AGENTS.md` map plus tests act as guides and sensors | Compare results with known gold outputs; measure pass^k across repeated runs; protect unit tests from agent edits |
| **AI-assisted apps** on Databricks foundation models (Genie, Agent Bricks, custom agents) | Follow the Genie order of instruction types; retrieve methodology documents just in time with AI Search rather than preloading them | Gateway quotas and budgets; guardrails; durable memory only for state that must persist. Inference logging stores whatever enters context, so keep personal data out | Genie benchmarks; [MLflow GenAI evaluation](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/mlflow3/genai/eval-monitor) with code scorers and judges; labeled cases where the app should ask for clarification or refuse |

Relevant Databricks references:
[Databricks Apps authorization](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/dev-tools/databricks-apps/auth),
[managed MCP servers](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/agents/mcp-tools/managed-mcp)
(Public Preview), and the
[Foundation Model APIs supported models](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/machine-learning/foundation-model-apis/supported-models)
page. Product names change often: Genie spaces are now called Genie Agents,
Vector Search is now AI Search, and AI Gateway is now Unity Gateway. Check each
docs page's preview banner before relying on a feature.

### Three cautions for marketing data

1. **Schema confusion is tool confusion.** Too many tables in scope degrade
   text-to-SQL the same way too many tools degrade tool choice. Curate.
2. **Client data in prompts is both a privacy risk and a cost.** Aggregate
   first, enforce minimum cell sizes, and use per-user authorization.
3. **Do not let the assistant grade its own narrative.** A deterministic check
   against the result table is cheaper and more reliable than asking a model
   whether its lift or overlap summary is correct.

## A minimal sketch: the number-check sensor

This illustrative check implements the third caution. It is an instructional
example, not tested production code, and the regular expression handles only
simple number formats.

```python
import re

import pandas as pd


def numbers_in_text(text: str) -> set[float]:
    """Extract plain numbers such as 12, 3.5, 1,200 or 45% from narrative text."""
    tokens = re.findall(r"-?\d[\d,]*\.?\d*", text)
    return {round(float(t.replace(",", "")), 2) for t in tokens}


def unsupported_numbers(narrative: str, result: pd.DataFrame) -> set[float]:
    """Return numbers in the narrative that do not appear in the result table."""
    numeric = result.select_dtypes("number").to_numpy().ravel()
    allowed = {round(float(x), 2) for x in numeric}
    allowed |= {round(float(x) * 100, 2) for x in numeric}  # shares shown as %
    return numbers_in_text(narrative) - allowed


result = pd.DataFrame({"segment": ["A", "B"], "overlap_rate": [0.18, 0.07]})
narrative = "Segment A overlaps 18% with the seed audience, versus 9% for B."
print(unsupported_numbers(narrative, result))  # {9.0} -> flag for review
```

In a harness, this check runs after the model writes its summary. If it finds
unsupported numbers, the app either asks the model to revise using only the
table or shows the table without the narrative.

## Exercise: audit one AI-assisted app

Choose an existing assistant or prototype and answer:

1. **Context inventory.** List everything in the context window on a typical
   request: system prompt, tool definitions, retrieved text, history. Estimate
   tokens for each. What could be removed or loaded just in time?
2. **Failure mapping.** Find one real failure and classify it as poisoning,
   distraction, confusion, or clash, or as a harness failure such as premature
   success or missing verification.
3. **One guide, one sensor.** Add one guide (a metric definition, example query,
   or `AGENTS.md` rule) and one computational sensor (a schema check, number
   check, or test).
4. **Measure.** Build 20 to 30 representative questions with known answers. Run
   each several times and report pass^k before and after your change, holding
   the model constant.

## Key takeaways

- **Context engineering** decides what the model sees at each step; **harness
  engineering** builds the system that makes many steps reliable.
- Treat *prompt ⊂ context ⊂ harness* as a useful heuristic, not an official
  taxonomy; the harness also includes deterministic parts that never enter the
  context.
- Context is a finite attention budget: more tokens can reduce quality. Use the
  four families—write, select, compress, isolate—and watch the cost trade-off
  with caching.
- Organize harness controls as guides and sensors, and prefer deterministic
  sensors where possible. Each harness component should fix a named failure.
- Benchmarks measure a model–harness pair. Hold one fixed when you evaluate the
  other, and report pass^k for reliability.
- On Databricks, governed metadata is the best context, deterministic functions
  and jobs are the best tools, and numbers should come from query results.
- Expect specific techniques and API names to expire; the separation of
  concerns is the durable lesson.
